stationClusters.name: Sonnblick Integrated CryoNet Cluster
stationClusters.description: The Sonnblick Observatory of ZAMG is located in the Austrian Central Alps at an elevation of 3100 m a.s.l. It was built in 1886 at the summit of Sonnblick Mountain, motivated by the need for information on meteorology in higher altitudes of the atmosphere. In 1986, the observatory was modernized with cable car access, electricity, and a large research platform for interdisciplinary research covering the atmosphere, atmospheric chemistry, the cryosphere, the biosphere, the lithosphere, and the hydrosphere. Sonnblick has long-term climate observations and studies on glacier changes and the impact of Climate Change on the cryosphere is a major topic. The research is described on www.sonnblick.net.  Sonnblick Observatory cooperates with Austrian and international universities/research institutions. Within the frame of the GAW-DACH cooperation, Sonnblick has partnered with the observatories Jungfraujoch (in Switzerland), Zugspitze and Hohenpeissenberg (both Germany). The observatory is part of the BSRN-Network.

stationClusters.name: Ny-Ålesund Integrated CryoNet Cluster
stationClusters.description: The Ny-Ålesund cluster is located on the Brøggerhalvøya peninsula and south coast of Kongsford in Svalbard, 79 degreees north in the Arctic. It is composed of three key research sites—Bayelva, Kvadehuken and Ny-Ålesund. The Bayelva Site has been monitored by the Alfred Wegener Institute since 1998 and records extensive soil, permafrost and meteorological variables. Kvadehuken features a 31 m deep permafrost borehole and a full-scale weather station at the western tip of the peninsula, and is part of the Climate-ecological Observatory for Arctic Tundra (COAT). Ny-Ålesund, established in 1951, was a pioneer station using automatic sensor systems, and provides long-term climate records. This cluster allows for comprehensive monitoring and modelling, enhancing understanding of cryosphere and climate dynamics in the High Arctic. Data flow from the cluster is in near-real time and coordinated by the Norwegian Meteorological Institute and visualized at cryo.met.no.

Eskdalemuir Observatory was established in 1908 to record geomagnetic observations. Initially the site was run by the National Physical Laboratory but it passed to the Meteorological Office in 1910. At that time it was thought that meteorology and geomagnetism were closely linked and so the site started to focus on a range of meteorological observations, becoming a first-order climatological and synoptic station. In May 1968 overall control passed to the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) but the Met Office kept staff on site to continue the synoptic and climatological data.
